study_identification.title: Dynamic gray matter volume changes in pediatric multiple sclerosis: A 3.5 year MRI study

study_characteristics.study_objective: To assess, using MRI, the spatial patterns of gray matter (GM) atrophy in pediatric patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), their dynamic changes over time, and their clinical relevance. The study aimed to determine whether disease onset during critical developmental periods affects physiologic trajectories of brain maturation.

dataset_name.answer: HSR (Hospital San Raffaele); NIH-funded MRI Study of Normal Brain Development

hc_age.answer: HSR HC: mean 15.4, sd 3.8; NIH HC: mean 10.8, sd 3.7; NIH HC age range: 4.2 to 22.3 years

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: SPM12; DARTEL (diffeomorphic anatomical registration using exponentiated lie algebra); Serial longitudinal registration; Lesion refilling; Segmentation; Modulation and smoothing with 4-mm Gaussian kernel

quality_checking_detail.answer: Quality check for motion and other artifacts was performed on NIH HC dataset. From all available HC initially downloaded, 317 were considered suitable for analysis after quality checking.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Magnetic field strength (MFS) included as a binary variable in linear mixed-effects model to account for differences in magnetic field strength and acquisition protocol between sites. Partial correlation analysis showed MFS had the lowest absolute r values (median [IQR] absolute r values: age = 0.16 [0.09-0.25], sex = 0.17 [0.13-0.21], age×sex = 0.11 [0.09-0.14], age² = 0.32 [0.20-0.39], MFS = 0.07 [0.03-0.11]; p < 0.0001). HSR data acquired at 3.0T (Philips) and NIH HC data acquired at 1.5T (GE and Siemens scanners at 6 pediatric centers).

software_tool.answer: Matlab 'fitlme' function (Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox); SPM12

response_variable.answer: Regional gray matter volume (voxel-level modulated GM images)

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Age²; Sex; Age×Sex interaction; Magnetic field strength (MFS)

predictor_effects.answer: Age, Age², Sex, Age×Sex interaction, and MFS modeled as fixed effects. Participant-specific random intercept (bi0) and random slope for age (bi1) included, assuming bivariate normal distribution for random effects vector, independent of homoscedastic normal error term.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses several important nuisance structures: (1) Magnetic field strength differences between 1.5T and 3.0T scanners are modeled as a fixed effect covariate; (2) Age nonlinearity is addressed through quadratic age term and age×sex interaction; (3) Sex differences in developmental trajectories are explicitly modeled; (4) Participant-specific heterogeneity is captured through random intercepts and slopes. However, the handling is incomplete because: (1) Multi-site effects within NIH dataset (6 different centers with different GE and Siemens scanners) are not explicitly modeled beyond MFS; (2) Potential heteroscedasticity (variance changing with age/sex) is not addressed - model assumes homoscedastic error; (3) No explicit discussion of whether residuals were examined for spatial autocorrelation or other model violations; (4) The paper does not report detailed model diagnostics or validation metrics.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To overcome potential biases, another binary variable to account for differences in magnetic field strength (MFSi) and acquisition protocol was also added. A bivariate normal distribution was assumed for the vector of random effects (bi0, bi1), independent of the homoscedastic normal error term. To explore the influence of magnetic field strength on HC developmental trajectory estimate, in comparison to the effect of interests, we derived partial correlation r maps for each regressor and compared the overall distributions of their absolute values by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. MFS showed the lowest absolute r values (median [interquartile range] absolute r values: age = 0.16 [0.09-0.25], sex = 0.17 [0.13-0.21], age×sex = 0.11 [0.09-0.14], age² = 0.32 [0.20-0.39], MFS = 0.07 [0.03-0.11]; p < 0.0001).
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Page with Methods section, Statistical analysis subsection / Lines 99-108

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validates the normative model using the same HC participants who were used for model training. The paper demonstrates model performance by: (1) Visualizing estimated developmental trajectories with individual participant data overlaid (spaghetti plots in Figure 1A); (2) Showing that model captures expected heterochronic maturational processes with different brain regions showing different developmental patterns; (3) Demonstrating sex-specific differences in developmental trajectories that align with known neurodevelopmental literature; (4) Showing that MFS effects are small compared to biological effects of interest. However, this is validation using the training data itself (non-independent), not held-out test data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: GM volume developmental trajectories as estimated in all HC are shown separately for male and female participants in figure 2. In line with previous studies, different GM developmental trajectories were found in male and female participants. Developmental trajectories were also different in the main brain regions, confirming the existence of a heterocronic maturational process. Brain regions showing negative GM volume change per year (growth rate) reached their maturational peak first, while brain regions showing a positive growth rate continued their maturation across the whole age range explored, in line with the inverted-U shape developmental trajectory described previously. (Figure 1A.a) Left thalamus GM developmental trajectories are represented as estimated in the whole group of healthy controls (means are represented by solid lines and 95% confidence interval by dashed lines). Spaghetti lines for each participant's measurement over time are also shown.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Results section, HC developmental trajectories / Lines 172-184; Figure 1A caption / Lines 113-115

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The paper does not report any hold-out validation or cross-validation approach. All available HC data (both HSR HC n=26 and NIH HC n=317) were used to estimate the normative developmental trajectories. There is no mention of splitting the HC data into training and test sets, no k-fold cross-validation, no leave-one-out validation, and no independent validation cohort from the same domain. The model was fit to all HC data and then applied directly to MS patients to calculate deviations.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: To estimate normative sex- and age-expected GM growth curves, using Matlab's 'fitlme' function (Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox), the following linear mixed-effects model was fitted voxel-wise to HC preprocessed GM maps: [model equation]. To overcome the difficulty of obtaining longitudinal MRI scans from pediatric HC, 2 groups of pediatric HC were selected for comparison of MRI volumes: (1) a group of 26 sex- and age-matched HC recruited at Hospital San Raffaele (HSR) with no history of neurologic dysfunction and a normal neurologic examination, studied on the same MRI scanner as patients with MS at baseline; and (2) a group of 317 pediatric HC from the NIH-funded MRI Study of Normal Brain Development (NIH HC) with longitudinal MRI assessments.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative model on any external independent dataset from a different domain (e.g., different scanner, different site, different country, different study). The normative model was built using HSR HC and NIH HC data, and was only applied to MS patients from the same institutions (HSR). There is no external validation on HC from completely independent studies or datasets to assess model generalizability.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes external validation on independent datasets from different domains. The study design section describes only two HC datasets used for model building, and the application is only to MS patients from HSR.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: N/A - information not present in manuscript

clinical_dataset.answer: Hospital San Raffaele (HSR) pediatric MS cohort

diseases_studied.answer: Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis (MS); Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS)

clinical_groups_n.answer: MS: 68 at baseline; MS with follow-up: 30

clinical_groups_age.answer: Baseline whole MS group: mean 15.1 years, sd 2.2; MS with FU: mean 15.5, sd 1.7; MS without FU: mean 14.7, sd 2.5

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores computed from sex- and age-specific, population-averaged, marginal mean and SD estimated from normative model. Z-scores represent standardized measure of deviation from normative expected GM volume at each voxel.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear models (SPM12) at baseline to estimate: (1) mean z-scores across whole MS group; (2) correlations between z-scores and disease duration, EDSS, premorbid IQ (full scale and subscales), T2 lesion volume, T1 lesion volume. Longitudinal analysis: Linear models adjusted for follow-up duration, baseline EDSS, and disease duration to estimate: (1) z-score changes over time; (2) correlations between z-score changes and baseline premorbid IQ, T2 LV changes, T1 LV changes. Multiple comparison correction: p<0.05 family-wise error (FWE) corrected; exploratory threshold p<0.001 uncorrected (cluster extent=50 voxels). Key findings: Higher EDSS correlated with more severe GM damage in bilateral thalamus, left caudate, left inferior frontal gyrus, right precuneus. Longer disease duration correlated with more severe GM damage in cingulate cortex, frontal and temporal regions. Higher IQ correlated with less severe GM damage and slower progression of deviations. Higher T2/T1 lesion volumes correlated with more severe GM damage in thalamus, caudate, frontal and temporal regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Pediatric MS patients showed widespread failures in GM development and progressive atrophy in cortical and subcortical regions, only partially related to focal WM lesions, suggesting early neurodegenerative phenomena; higher IQ was protective.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: At baseline, pediatric MS patients (n=68) showed significant GM volume deviations (reductions) from sex- and age-expected trajectories in multiple regions including basal ganglia (thalamus, caudate), hippocampus, and extensive cortical areas in frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes, as well as cerebellum (p<0.05 FWE corrected; Table 2 lists 38 distinct regions). Longitudinally (n=30, median 3.5 year follow-up), patients showed progression of GM atrophy in most baseline-affected regions (bilateral thalamus, putamen, supplementary motor area, precuneus, multiple frontal/parietal/temporal/occipital regions), but also showed reduced deviation (improvement) in several left parietal and temporal regions and right occipital regions (p<0.001 uncorrected; Table 4). Correlations with clinical measures: Higher EDSS correlated with more severe atrophy in thalamus (L: r=-0.42, R: r=-0.38), caudate (L: r=-0.45), inferior frontal gyrus (L: r=-0.46), and precuneus (R: r=-0.42). Higher premorbid IQ full scale score correlated with less severe baseline deviations in multiple regions (r=0.45-0.60, strongest in gyrus rectus r=0.60 and frontal regions r=0.51-0.59) and slower progression over time (r=0.51-0.63, strongest in inferior temporal gyrus r=0.63, superior frontal gyrus R r=0.63). Higher T2 and T1 lesion volumes correlated with more severe thalamic atrophy (T2 LV: R r=-0.55, L r=-0.54; T1 LV: R r=-0.59, L r=-0.58, p<0.05 FWE corrected). Lesion volume changes over time correlated with progression in thalamus, precentral and postcentral gyri (T2 LV change with precentral gyrus r=-0.63; T1 LV change with postcentral gyrus L r=-0.71, thalamus R r=-0.70). Notably, many regions showed GM damage not associated with focal WM lesions, suggesting primary GM involvement. EDSS remained stable during follow-up (median 1.0, p=0.28), while T1 LV increased significantly (p=0.03).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, only 30 of 68 patients underwent follow-up assessment (28 refused, 10 had recent baseline with <1 year follow-up), resulting in a relatively small longitudinal sample despite pediatric MS rarity. Second, only IQ was analyzed as a measure of cognitive reserve; other factors such as socioeconomic characteristics and leisure activities were not collected and should be included in future studies. Third, the clinical stability of patients during study period (EDSS remained stable, median annualized relapse rate 0) did not allow analysis of prediction of disability worsening, requiring longer follow-up to ascertain clinical relevance of GM volumetric abnormalities. Fourth, while the study controlled for magnetic field strength differences, the difficulty of obtaining longitudinal scans in pediatric HC necessitated use of a multi-site historical cohort (NIH dataset) rather than perfectly matched local controls. Fifth, intracranial volume was not included in models because previous studies showed brain-skull growth dissociation in pediatric MS, making skull-based normalization unreliable.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that expected resilience to CNS injury and greater repair potential in pediatric patients are not sufficient to prevent GM atrophy. Authors emphasize importance of therapeutic strategies focused on neuroprotection and neurorepair to prevent long-term disability accrual. The finding that some regions showed reduced deviation over time (potential recovery or reaching atrophy plateau) raises interesting questions about plasticity and reparative mechanisms in young patients, though pathologic confirmation is needed. Authors note that focal GM lesions are relatively rare in pediatric MS and unlikely to explain volumetric abnormalities. The protective effect of higher IQ may reflect cognitive reserve promoting remodeling of GM pruning processes. The study used a sophisticated voxel-wise approach with linear mixed-effects modeling to trace spatial patterns of GM changes, accounting for the complex interplay between normal development, disease pathology, and brain plasticity during critical maturational periods.

general_notes.general_notes:
This is a pediatric multiple sclerosis neuroimaging study that applies normative modeling methodology to understand deviations from typical brain development. The normative modeling approach is central to the study design - the authors explicitly built sex- and age-specific normative developmental trajectories from healthy controls and then quantified patient-specific deviations (z-scores) at the voxel level. This represents an important application of normative modeling to pediatric neurological disease.

Key methodological considerations:

1. Dataset composition: The normative model combined two HC datasets - local HSR controls (n=26, 3.0T Philips) matched to patient scanner, and a large multi-site historical cohort (NIH dataset, n=317, 1.5T GE/Siemens from 6 centers). This pragmatic approach was necessary due to difficulty obtaining longitudinal pediatric HC data, but introduces heterogeneity.

2. Modeling approach: Voxel-wise linear mixed-effects models with quadratic age term, sex, age×sex interaction, and MFS covariate. Random intercepts and slopes for participants captured individual variability. The model equation: Yij = β0 + β1*Ageij + β2*Sexi + β3*Ageij*Sexi + β4*Age²ij + β5*MFSi + bi0 + bi1*Ageij + εij.

3. Preprocessing: Sophisticated longitudinal pipeline using SPM12 with within-subject serial registration, DARTEL for groupwise alignment, lesion refilling, tissue segmentation, modulation by Jacobian determinants, and 4-mm smoothing. This approach maintains longitudinal consistency while normalizing to MNI space.

4. Clinical relevance: The study found that GM damage in deep GM structures (thalamus, caudate) was most strongly associated with disability, while higher cognitive reserve (IQ) was protective against both baseline atrophy and longitudinal progression. This suggests normative modeling can identify clinically meaningful deviations.

5. WM lesion relationships: Importantly, only partial correlations were found between focal WM lesion burden and GM atrophy, particularly in highly connected regions (thalamus, basal ganglia, sensorimotor cortex). Many regions showed GM damage independent of WM lesions, suggesting primary GM pathology rather than secondary Wallerian degeneration alone.

6. Developmental context: The study beautifully demonstrates heterochronic brain maturation with region-specific developmental trajectories following a posterior-to-anterior, phylogenetically-based sequence. Sex differences in maturation were prominent, with divergence starting around puberty (12 years), underscoring the importance of sex-stratified or sex-adjusted models in pediatric populations.

7. Bidirectional longitudinal changes: Interestingly, some regions showed progression of deviations (worsening atrophy) while others showed reduction of deviations (partial recovery or plateau), raising important questions about plasticity, repair mechanisms, and age-dependent vulnerability to MS pathology.

8. Validation limitations: While the model captured expected developmental patterns consistent with neurodevelopmental literature, no formal cross-validation or external validation was performed. Model diagnostics (residual plots, goodness-of-fit metrics like explained variance, MSLL, or distributional properties of z-scores in HC) were not reported.

9. Statistical thresholds: Results reported at FWE p<0.05 for strong effects and p<0.001 uncorrected for exploratory analyses. The exploratory threshold was necessary due to small longitudinal sample (n=30) but increases risk of false positives.

10. All study participants were Caucasian, limiting generalizability to other ethnic groups.

11. Treatment context: All patients were on disease-modifying treatments at baseline (interferon-β=41, glatiramer acetate=16, natalizumab=11) and none changed treatment during follow-up, so effects of treatment on developmental trajectories could not be assessed.

12. IQ findings: 16 patients (23%) had low IQ (70-90 range), but baseline IQ was only different between FU and non-FU groups for performance IQ subscale (p=0.02), not total or verbal IQ.

This study exemplifies application of normative modeling to pediatric neurological populations where distinguishing disease effects from developmental variation is critical. The approach allowed identification of disease-related deviations from expected maturational trajectories that correlated with clinical disability and cognitive reserve, providing insights into pathophysiology and potential protective factors.
